title: Single Administration of Bimatoprost Implant Effects on 24-Hour Intraocular Pressure and 1-Year Outcomes
article_subtype: Multicenter, open-label phase 3b clinical study with 12-month follow-up
condition_or_topic: 24-hour intraocular pressure control with a single bimatoprost implant administration in adults with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension.
clinical_background: Lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) is intended to reduce glaucomatous visual field loss, but IOP varies with body position and circadian timing. Peaks can occur outside office hours and are likely to contribute to glaucoma progression, making daytime and nighttime control relevant. Some topical IOP-lowering drug classes have diminished nighttime efficacy, whereas topical prostaglandin analogs/prostamides, including bimatoprost, have lowered IOP over 24 hours. Earlier phase 3 studies found that a single 10- or 15-mg bimatoprost implant was noninferior to twice-daily topical timolol maleate 0.5% for IOP lowering through 12 weeks, but its effects outside usual office hours had not been reported.
objectives: Primarily, assess hour-matched change from baseline in study-eye IOP in the habitual position across 24 hours at week 8 after a single 10-mg bimatoprost implant administration, using pneumatonometry.
Assess change from baseline in the range of habitual-position IOP over 24 hours at week 8.
Assess hour-matched IOP change from baseline in the supine position at week 8.
Assess change from baseline in hour 0 IOP by Goldmann applanation tonometry and time to first use of additional IOP-lowering treatment through month 12.
Assess safety through 12 months, including treatment-emergent adverse events and central corneal endothelial cell density.
clinical_question: In adults with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension requiring IOP-lowering treatment, how does a single intracameral 10-mg bimatoprost implant change habitual-position IOP across 24 hours at week 8 compared with baseline, and what are its IOP-lowering and safety outcomes through 12 months?
interpretation: In patients with OAG or OHT, a single administration of the bimatoprost implant lowered habitual-position IOP during both daytime and nighttime at week 8 and reduced 24-hour IOP fluctuation. Mean IOP reductions were 2.6 mmHg during the diurnal period and 2.1 mmHg during the nocturnal period. Most participants maintained lower IOP without additional treatment through 1 year; 74% (23/31) had not needed further IOP-lowering treatment in the study eye. The authors considered the safety profile favorable after a single administration: no implant-treated eye had a CECD loss of 15% or greater at 1 year, and no adverse event required implant removal or caused study discontinuation. They propose that prolonged IOP lowering after drug depletion may result from enhanced matrix metalloproteinase activation and lasting remodeling of aqueous outflow pathways, rather than establishing this mechanism in the present study.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier studies of once-daily topical bimatoprost 0.01% found daytime IOP reductions approximately twice the nighttime reductions; the authors interpret the present implant findings as showing a more sustained effect across 24 hours, while noting that this study does not support a direct comparison between its treatment groups. Prior research identified long-term IOP fluctuation as a risk factor for glaucomatous progression, whereas a contribution from short-term (24-hour) fluctuation remains a possibility. Unlike the implant group, the small topical reference cohort showed no reduction in 24-hour fluctuation; the authors note that its size may account for this finding because earlier studies suggested that topical PGAs, including bimatoprost, reduce such fluctuation. The approximately 7 mmHg reduction measured by GAT at week 8 was consistent with the phase 3 ARTEMIS studies. Sustained lowering was also consistent with an earlier phase 1/2 implant study in which 28% (21/75) of participants receiving a 6-, 10-, 15-, or 20-mg implant completed 24 months without rescue topical medication or another implant. In the phase 3 ARTEMIS studies, approximately 5% of participants receiving 3 administrations of the 10-mg implant at fixed 16-week intervals had CECD loss of 20% or greater within 1 year; those studies reported no adverse events of corneal endothelial cell loss before the second administration.
clinical_implications: After a single implant administration, patients may have a high probability of needing no other IOP-lowering treatment for at least 1 year.

The authors note that larger CECD losses can be associated with reduced corneal transparency, corneal edema, and poorer visual acuity, whereas a loss of 10% or less may reflect measurement error or lack clinical significance.
limitations: The study had a small sample.
Nocturnal IOP effects during undisturbed sleep were not assessed.
The reference cohort was very small, came from a single site, and was not assigned randomly; the design therefore did not permit a direct comparison with the implant group.
Pneumatonometry and GAT measurements at hour 0 were obtained on different days by different assessors and cannot be compared directly.
Office-visit IOP assessments were unmasked, although a 2-person reading method was used to reduce potential bias.
Long-term efficacy and safety were not collected for the reference cohort because its participation ended after 8 weeks.
strengths: For each participant, one masked assessor used the same pneumatonometer for all sleep-lab IOP measurements, permitting habitual-position assessments without introducing differences between daytime and nighttime measurements from using different tonometry methods.
open_questions: The reason office-visit and sleep-lab IOP measurements differed remains unknown.
study_design: Multicenter, open-label, 12-month phase 3b study (NCT04285580) conducted at 5 sites from June 11, 2020, to May 14, 2022. Participants received bimatoprost implant; an investigator-assigned, nonrandomized reference cohort at 1 site received topical bimatoprost 0.01%. The study was not powered to compare the groups statistically.

population.description: Nonsmoking adults with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension requiring IOP-lowering treatment in at least 1 eye. The bimatoprost implant group included 31 participants, and the reference cohort included 6. If both eyes qualified, the eye with higher baseline hour 0 IOP was selected; when IOP was equal, the right eye was selected.
inclusion_criteria: Diagnosis of open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension requiring IOP-lowering treatment in at least 1 eye.
Open iridocorneal angle in the study eye on clinical gonioscopy.
Study-eye IOP after medication washout of 22 to 34 mmHg by GAT.
exclusion_criteria: Previous bimatoprost implant administration in the study eye.
Previous laser trabeculoplasty in the study eye.
History or evidence of clinically relevant substantial ocular trauma in the study eye.
History or evidence of complicated cataract surgery or phakic intraocular lens insertion to correct refractive error in the study eye.
population.mean_age: 70.4 (11.2) years, mean (SD) in the total population
population.care_setting: Office visits and sleep-laboratory visits across 5 sites.

interventions: A single intracameral 10-mg bimatoprost implant was administered to the study eye on day 1 using a prefilled, single-use, 28-gauge applicator; 31 participants received the implant.
comparators: At 1 site, an investigator-assigned reference cohort of 6 participants received topical bimatoprost 0.01% in the study eye once daily at 8 PM 1 hour, beginning on day 1. This cohort exited after the week 8 sleep-laboratory visit.

primary: Hour-matched change from baseline in study-eye IOP at week 8, measured by pneumatonometry in the habitual position: sitting from 8 AM to 10 PM and supine from 12 AM to 6 AM.
secondary: Change from baseline at week 8 in the range of habitual-position IOP measurements in implant-treated study eyes, evaluated across the diurnal, nocturnal and entire 24-hour periods.
Hour-matched change from baseline in supine-position IOP at the week 8 sleep-laboratory visit.
Change from baseline through month 12 in hour 0 (8 AM) IOP measured by GAT at office visits.
Time from implant administration to first use of nonstudy rescue IOP-lowering medication and/or a procedure.

Safety assessments, including treatment-emergent adverse events, best-corrected visual acuity, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, dilated ophthalmoscopy, visual fields, pachymetry, gonioscopy and implant assessment, and central corneal endothelial cell density.

statistical_methods: For the implant group, mean hour-matched changes from baseline in habitual-position IOP were calculated at 12 timepoints over 24 hours, with 95% confidence intervals based on paired t tests. IOP fluctuation was assessed using each participant’s range of measurements during the diurnal, nocturnal and full 24-hour periods. Time to initial rescue treatment was estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method. Efficacy analyses used participants who received study treatment and had at least 1 postbaseline study-eye IOP assessment; measurements after rescue treatment began were excluded. Safety analyses included all participants who received study treatment. The primary and secondary efficacy analyses used the first planned database lock, after the week 8 sleep-laboratory visits; other efficacy and safety analyses used the final lock. Sample size was chosen on practical grounds rather than to power a statistical comparison between groups.
follow_up: The implant group was followed through month 12, with safety assessment on day 2 and day 8, office visits at week 8, week 16, and months 6, 9, and 12, and a week 8 sleep-laboratory visit. The reference cohort was followed until its week 8 sleep-laboratory visit.

main_conclusion: The authors concluded that one administration of bimatoprost implant lowered IOP across daytime and nighttime at week 8 and reduced 24-hour IOP fluctuation. Most participants maintained IOP lowering without additional treatment through 1 year, with a favorable safety profile after a single administration.
narrative_summary:
This multicenter, open-label phase 3b study evaluated a single intracameral administration of bimatoprost implant 10 mg in adults with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension. The implant group comprised 31 participants, all of whom completed the 12-month study. Pneumatonometry measured IOP every 2 hours over 24 hours at baseline and week 8, with participants sitting during daytime habitual-position assessments and supine overnight. Office visits used Goldmann applanation tonometry to assess IOP through month 12. A small cohort received topical bimatoprost 0.01% as a reference; the study was not designed for direct comparison between groups.

At week 8, implant-treated eyes had lower IOP throughout both day and night. Their mean 24-hour IOP range decreased from 9.9 (4.22) mmHg at baseline to 8.3 (3.50) mmHg, a change of -1.6 (2.98) mmHg that arose chiefly during daytime assessments. At month 12, 23/31 participants had required no rescue IOP-lowering treatment; in these nonrescued eyes, mean IOP change from baseline was -4.3 (3.35) mmHg. Conjunctival hyperemia was the most common TEAE, occurring in 11 (35.5) participants. No implant-treated eye had a 15% loss of CECD from baseline. The authors considered the findings supportive of sustained IOP lowering after one administration, while noting the small sample and the inability to assess nocturnal IOP during undisturbed sleep.

safety_results.discontinuations: No participant discontinued the study because of a TEAE, and no implant removal was required.
notable_adverse_events: Conjunctival hyperemia: 11 (35.5) in the bimatoprost implant 10 mg group (N = 31).

Intraocular pressure increased: 7 (22.6) in the bimatoprost implant 10 mg group (N = 31). Among the 7 reports, 4 involved only the study eye, 2 involved both eyes at the sleep-lab visit, and 1 involved only the fellow eye receiving standard-of-care treatment. The study-eye events could have reflected waning of the implant's IOP-lowering effect.
Conjunctival hemorrhage: 3 (9.7) in the bimatoprost implant 10 mg group (N = 31).

Visual field defect: 3 (9.7) in the bimatoprost implant 10 mg group (N = 31). One report concerned mild nasal-step progression in the study eye that the investigator considered unrelated to treatment; the other 2 concerned fellow eyes receiving standard-of-care treatment.
Cataract: 2 (6.5) in the bimatoprost implant 10 mg group (N = 31).
Dry eye: 2 (6.5) in the bimatoprost implant 10 mg group (N = 31).
Foreign body sensation in eye: 2 (6.5) in the bimatoprost implant 10 mg group (N = 31).
Punctate keratitis: 2 (6.5) in the bimatoprost implant 10 mg group (N = 31).
COVID-19: 2 (6.5) in the bimatoprost implant 10 mg group (N = 31). The sole serious TEAE was a case of coronavirus disease 19 considered unrelated to treatment.
All reported TEAEs were mild or moderate; most treatment-related TEAEs were associated with the administration procedure.

In implant-treated study eyes, mean change in CECD from baseline at month 12 was -53.0 (95.74) cells/mm2, corresponding to a 2% mean decrease over 12 months. No eye had a 15% loss from baseline, and no clinically significant CECD change was observed.
Safety assessments identified no concerns involving best-corrected visual acuity, visual fields, lens opacity, cup/disc ratio, central corneal thickness, CECD, or gonioscopy and implant assessments.

secondary_results: In the bimatoprost implant 10 mg group (n = 31), the mean diurnal sitting IOP range was 7.7 (3.89) mmHg at baseline and 5.8 (2.33) mmHg at week 8; mean change from baseline at week 8 was -2.0 (3.41) mmHg.

In the bimatoprost implant 10 mg group (n = 31), the mean nocturnal supine IOP range was 4.7 (2.06) mmHg at baseline and 4.6 (3.76) mmHg at week 8; mean change from baseline at week 8 was -0.1 (3.87) mmHg. The reduction in the 24-hour range occurred primarily during the day.

In the topical bimatoprost 0.01% reference cohort, mean change from baseline in the 24-hour habitual-position IOP range at week 8 was +0.7 (3.90) mmHg (median: -0.5 mmHg; n = 5). The authors did not observe a reduction in this cohort and noted that its small size could explain that result.
At the baseline hour-0 office visit, mean IOP by GAT was 24.2 (2.70) mmHg in the implant group, 25.3 (3.14) mmHg in the topical bimatoprost QD group, and 24.4 (2.76) mmHg in the total population.

For implant-treated study eyes at 8 AM, mean IOP by GAT at the office visit was 24.2 (2.70) mmHg at baseline and 17.4 (2.83) mmHg at week 8; mean change from baseline was -6.8 (3.13) mmHg. At the sleep-lab visit, mean sitting IOP by pneumatonometry was 25.3 (7.15) mmHg at baseline and 21.5 (3.74) mmHg at week 8; mean change was -3.7 (5.65) mmHg. Both methods showed IOP lowering, although measurements differed between visits.

At week 8, pneumatonometry also showed lower IOP at each daytime timepoint in implant-treated eyes when participants were supine as well as sitting; numerical results for those timepoints were not provided.

The bimatoprost implant group enrolled 31 participants, all of whom received an implant and completed the 12-month study; mean study duration was 361.7 days (range, 351e379 days). The reference group enrolled 6 participants, all of whom received topical bimatoprost 0.01%; 5 (83.3%) completed the week 8 visit and exited as planned, while 1 (16.7%) stopped early because of an excluded medication. Mean reference-group study duration was 57.5 days (range, 56e60 days). All 37 participants entered the full efficacy analysis set.

At baseline, mean age was 70.5 (11.8) years in the implant group, 70.2 (8.5) years in the topical bimatoprost QD group, and 70.4 (11.2) years overall; the respective age ranges were 40e90, 59e78, and 40e90 years. Participants in the age category labeled 65 yrs, % numbered 21 (67.7), 4 (66.7), and 25 (67.6), respectively.

At baseline, male participants numbered 13 (41.9) in the implant group, 4 (66.7) in the topical bimatoprost QD group, and 17 (45.9) overall; female participants numbered 18 (58.1), 2 (33.3), and 20 (54.1), respectively.

At baseline, White participants numbered 22 (71.0) in the implant group, 4 (66.7) in the topical bimatoprost QD group, and 26 (70.3) overall. The corresponding counts for Black or African American participants were 7 (22.6), 1 (16.7), and 8 (21.6); for Asian participants, 2 (6.5), 1 (16.7), and 3 (8.1); and for Hispanic participants, 3 (9.7), 0 (0), and 3 (8.1).

For study-eye diagnosis at baseline, POAG was recorded in 25 (80.6) implant-group participants, 3 (50.0) topical bimatoprost QD participants, and 28 (75.7) participants overall; OHT was recorded in 6 (19.4), 3 (50.0), and 9 (24.3), respectively.

At baseline, phakic study eyes numbered 20 (64.5) in the implant group, 4 (66.7) in the topical bimatoprost QD group, and 24 (64.9) overall; pseudophakic study eyes numbered 11 (35.5), 2 (33.3), and 13 (35.1), respectively. Mean CECD (SD) was 2680 (234), 2779 (255), and 2696 (237) cells/mm2, respectively.

Gonioscopic assessment of implant size showed swelling to an estimated 101% to 150% of initial size in 38.7% (12/31) of implants at week 16. By month 12, 67.7% (21/31) were no longer visible or were estimated to be 25% of initial size, 29.0% (9/31) were estimated to be 25% to 50%, and 3.2% (1/31) were estimated to be 50% to 75%.

document_sections.heading: Purpose
document_sections.content: The study assessed how one bimatoprost implant administration affected intraocular pressure (IOP) across 24 hours at 8 weeks, as well as IOP control and safety through 1 year.

document_sections.heading: Design
document_sections.content: This was a multicenter, open-label, 12-month, phase 3b study registered as NCT04285580.

document_sections.heading: Participants
document_sections.content: Participants were adults with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: Participants (n = 31) received a 10-mg bimatoprost implant in the study eye on day 1. Pneumatonometry measured seated and/or supine IOP every 2 hours over 24 hours at baseline and week 8. Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT) measured IOP at hour 0, within 1 hour of 8 AM, at baseline, weeks 8 and 16, and months 6, 9, and 12.

document_sections.heading: Main Outcome Measures
document_sections.content: The primary endpoint was the baseline-to-week-8 change in habitual-position IOP at corresponding hours across 24 hours, measured by pneumatonometry. Through 12 months, the investigators also assessed hour-0 GAT IOP change in eyes without additional IOP-lowering treatment, treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), and central corneal endothelial cell density (CECD).

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: At baseline, mean IOP (standard deviation [SD]) at hour 0 was 24.2 (2.70) mmHg by GAT and 25.3 (7.15) mmHg by pneumatonometry. At week 8, habitual-position pneumatonometry showed IOP reductions throughout daytime and nighttime and less IOP fluctuation; habitual position meant sitting from 8 AM to 10 PM and supine from 12 AM to 6 AM. The mean (SD) reduction from baseline in the 24-hour IOP range was 1.6 (2.98) mmHg. All 31 implant-treated participants finished the 12-month study, and 23 (74%) needed no rescue IOP-lowering treatment. Among eyes without rescue treatment, mean (SD) IOP reduction from baseline at month 12 was 4.3 (3.35) mmHg. Conjunctival hyperemia was the most frequent TEAE, with an incidence of 35.5% (11/31). No implant-treated eye lost 15% of its baseline CECD.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: At week 8, one intracameral bimatoprost implant administration lowered habitual-position IOP throughout daytime and nighttime. Most participants maintained lower IOP for 1 year without further treatment. The authors characterized safety through 1 year as favorable.

document_sections.heading: Single Administration of Bimatoprost Implant Effects on 24-Hour Intraocular Pressure and 1-Year Outcomes
document_sections.content: Glaucoma treatment lowers IOP to decrease the risk of glaucomatous visual-field loss. Body position and circadian rhythm affect IOP, and both people with elevated IOP and normal controls experience daytime and nighttime variation. IOP peaks often fall outside office hours and are likely to contribute to glaucoma progression, making control across day and night important. Some topical IOP-lowering drug classes, including beta-blockers, have less nighttime efficacy; earlier studies found that topical prostaglandin analogs/prostamides (PGAs), including bimatoprost, lower IOP over 24 hours. Bimatoprost implant 10 mg (Durysta; Allergan, an AbbVie company) is a biodegradable treatment for open-angle glaucoma (OAG) or ocular hypertension (OHT). It contains 10 mg of bimatoprost in a poly-lactic acid and polylactic-co-glycolic polymer matrix. The rod measures approximately 200 mm in diameter and 1.1 mm in length, as rendered in the article. Following intracameral placement with a prefilled, single-use, 28-gauge applicator, it releases bimatoprost continuously for approximately 3 to 4 months while its polymers hydrolyze and are metabolized to carbon dioxide and water. Two similarly designed phase 3 studies found that one administration of either a 10- or 15-mg implant was noninferior to twice-daily topical timolol maleate 0.5% for IOP reduction through 12 weeks; those studies used GAT at hour 0, within 1 hour of 8 AM, and hour 2 at baseline and weeks 2, 6, and 12. An earlier phase 1/2 study of 6, 10, 15, and 20 mg implant strengths found that baseline-to-follow-up IOP changes measured from 10 AM to 4 PM were consistent with the change at its primary 8 AM measurement. The authors stated that implant effects outside usual office hours had not previously been reported to their knowledge. They noted US Food and Drug Administration approval of one intracameral 10 mg implant administration per eye to lower IOP in OAG and OHT. Their primary objective was to assess 24-hour IOP lowering by pneumatonometry at 8 weeks after one 10-mg implant in patients with OAG or OHT; pneumatonometry enabled supine measurements. They also planned GAT assessment of hour-0 IOP lowering and safety through 12 months.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The investigators conducted a multicenter study at 5 sites. It was open-label, lasted 12 months, and was designated phase 3b; its purpose was to examine implant-associated IOP lowering across 24 hours in OAG or OHT. The study ran from June 11, 2020, to May 14, 2022, under the Declaration of Helsinki and the Health Information Portability and Accountability Act. Each site obtained institutional review board or ethics committee approval, and participants gave written consent before screening. Its ClinicalTrials.gov identifier was NCT04285580.

document_sections.heading: Participants
document_sections.content: Eligible participants were nonsmoking adults diagnosed with OAG or OHT who needed IOP-lowering therapy in at least 1 eye. The study eye required an open iridocorneal angle on clinical gonioscopy and a post-washout baseline GAT IOP of 22 to 34 mmHg. Principal exclusions were a previous bimatoprost implant or laser trabeculoplasty in the study eye, clinically relevant substantial trauma of that eye, and complicated cataract surgery or phakic intraocular lens insertion to correct refractive error in that eye. Table S1 contains the complete eligibility criteria. If both eyes qualified, the eye with higher baseline hour-0 IOP was selected; a tie was resolved in favor of the right eye. Participants were offered compensation for travel and time at study visits.

document_sections.heading: Study Design
document_sections.content: After screening, potentially eligible patients stopped IOP-lowering medications in both eyes. Minimum washout was 4 days for parasympathomimetics and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, 14 days for sympathomimetics and alpha agonists, and 28 days for b-blockers, r kinase inhibitors, and PGAs. Eligible patients underwent baseline office assessments followed by a 24-hour sleep-lab IOP assessment within the next 7 days. On day 1 after that visit, the study eye received a 10-mg bimatoprost implant intracamerally under standard aseptic conditions, using sterile technique and a prefilled, single-use, 28-gauge applicator. Safety checks occurred at an office visit on day 2 and by telephone on day 8. The week 8 office visit preceded a sleep-lab visit by no more than 7 days; further office follow-up occurred at week 16 and months 6, 9, and 12, with study exit at month 12. At 1 site, investigators assigned a separate reference cohort to topical bimatoprost 0.01% in the study eye once daily at 8 PM within 1 hour, beginning on day 1. That cohort left the study following its week 8 sleep-lab visit. Fellow eyes received standard-of-care care throughout, provided the investigator knew of no crossover effect on the study eye. At baseline and week 8 sleep-lab visits, a staff member masked to treatment and study eye used a Reichert Model 30 pneumatonometer to obtain IOP measurements every 2 hours across 24 hours, at 8 AM, 10 AM, 12 PM, 2 PM, 4 PM, 6 PM, 8 PM, 10 PM, 12 AM, 2 AM, 4 AM, and 6 AM, each within 30 minutes of the scheduled time. For daytime measurements from 8 AM to 10 PM, participants first rested supine for 5 minutes and were measured, then rested seated for 5 minutes before habitual-position measurement. Individual sleep-room lights went off at 11 PM. Nighttime measurements from 12 AM to 6 AM took place under dim light after 5 minutes of rest in the habitual supine position. At office visits, seated hour-0 IOP was measured by GAT around 8 AM, within 1 hour, using a 2-person reading method. Both settings measured the right eye before the left. Each eye had 2 readings; a difference > 1 mmHg prompted a third. Analysis used the mean of 2 readings or the median of 3. Office safety evaluations covered TEAEs, best-corrected visual acuity, slit-lamp examination, dilated ophthalmoscopy, visual fields, pachymetry, gonioscopy, and implant assessment. Investigators measured central CECD with specular microscopy and automated analysis. They could start rescue IOP-lowering treatment in the study eye when, in their judgment, inadequate IOP control made it necessary for participant safety.

document_sections.heading: Outcome Measures
document_sections.content: The primary efficacy measure was change from baseline to week 8 in study-eye IOP at corresponding hours, measured by pneumatonometry in the habitual position: seated from 8 AM to 10 PM and supine from 12 AM to 6 AM. The secondary efficacy measure was change in the study-eye IOP range at the week 8 sleep-lab assessment after implant treatment. Other prespecified measures were matched-hour changes in supine IOP at that visit, baseline-to-follow-up change in office GAT hour-0 IOP through month 12, and time until first nonstudy rescue IOP-lowering treatment.

document_sections.heading: Data Analysis
document_sections.content: The plan specified 2 database locks: one after the final remaining participant completed the week 8 sleep-lab visit and another at study completion. The first supplied primary and secondary efficacy analyses; the final lock supplied the other efficacy and safety analyses. The full efficacy analysis set comprised intervention recipients, whether assigned an implant or topical bimatoprost 0.01%, with at least 1 postbaseline study-eye IOP assessment usable for efficacy analysis. Readings obtained after rescue treatment began in an eye were excluded to prevent confounding. The safety population included everyone who received a study intervention. Primary analysis examined habitual-position daytime and nighttime IOP, and matched-hour change from baseline, by visit and timepoint. For implant-treated study eyes, investigators calculated mean matched-hour IOP changes at 12 timepoints across 24 hours, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) based on paired t tests. Secondary analysis quantified each participant’s habitual-position IOP range over the daytime waking interval of 8 AM to 10 PM, nighttime sleep interval of 12 AM to 6 AM, and full 8 AM to 6 AM measurement cycle. Kaplan-Meier estimation evaluated time from implantation to first rescue medication and/or procedure.

document_sections.heading: Sample Size Determination
document_sections.content: Sample size reflected practical considerations rather than power for a between-group comparison. The plan called for approximately 35 participants: 25 to 30 implant recipients and 5 reference-cohort participants. Enrolling 25 to 30 implant recipients was expected to leave a minimum of 20 with adequate baseline and week 8 measurements for evaluation of 24-hour IOP lowering, assuming premature discontinuation of up to 33%. The study was not powered to statistically compare implant and reference cohorts.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: The implant group enrolled 31 patients; every participant received a 10 mg implant in the study eye and completed the 12-month study. Mean study duration was 361.7 days (range, 351–379 days). At one site, 6 patients entered the reference group and all received once-daily topical bimatoprost 0.01% in the study eye. Of these, 5 (83.3%) completed the week 8 visit and exited as planned; 1 (16.7%) left early because of an excluded medication. Reference-group mean study duration was 57.5 days (range, 56–60 days). All 37 participants entered the full efficacy analysis set. Table 2 presents baseline participant and study-eye characteristics for the implant group, reference group, and overall population. The implant group resembled the overall population demographically and ophthalmically. Implant recipients had a mean age of 70.5 years (range, 40–90 years); 58.1% (18/31) were female, 71.0% (22/31) were White, and 80.6% (25/31) had primary OAG in the study eye. Age and race were similar in the reference cohort, where most participants were male (66.7%, 4/6) and 50% (3/6) had study-eye OHT. At week 8, pneumatonometry showed lower habitual-position IOP across day and night after implantation. For implant-treated study eyes (n = 31), reported mean matched-hour change across 24 hours ranged from 3.7 to -1.7 mmHg; the daytime seated range was -3.7 to -1.8 mmHg and the nighttime supine range was -2.4 to -1.7 mmHg. For topical bimatoprost 0.01% reference eyes (n = 5), the corresponding 24-hour range was -5.0 to -1.8 mmHg, with reductions throughout daytime. Habitual-position IOP variation also decreased after implantation: the mean 24-hour range was 9.9 mmHg at baseline versus 8.3 mmHg at week 8, a mean change of -1.6 mmHg. Table 3 presents the baseline, week 8, and change values for 24-hour, seated daytime, and supine nighttime IOP ranges. Reduced daytime variation accounted for most of the 24-hour change. In reference eyes treated with bimatoprost 0.01%, mean (SD) change in the 24-hour habitual-position IOP range at week 8 was +0.7 (3.90) mmHg (median: -0.5 mmHg; n = 5). Office GAT and sleep-lab pneumatonometry gave somewhat different measurements, as Table 4 shows. For implant-treated eyes at 8 AM in week 8, mean (SD) change from baseline was -6.8 (3.1) mmHg by office GAT and -3.7 (5.7) mmHg by seated sleep-lab pneumatonometry. Pneumatonometry also showed week 8 reductions at every daytime timepoint with participants supine as well as seated; Table S5 presents those measurements. Most implant-treated eyes maintained lower IOP without rescue through the month 12 exit visit. No rescue was required by 100% (31/31) at week 8 and by 74.2% (23/31) at month 12. Among implant-treated eyes without rescue at month 12 (n = 23), mean (SD) baseline-to-month-12 GAT IOP change was -4.3 (3.35) mmHg. Kaplan-Meier estimates of remaining free of study-eye rescue treatment after implantation were 84% at 120 days (approximately 4 months), 81% at 180 days (approximately 6 months), and 74% at both 270 days and 360 days (approximately 9 and 12 months, respectively). Table 6 presents implant-group TEAEs with incidence > 5%: conjunctival hyperemia, increased IOP, conjunctival hemorrhage, visual-field defect, cataract, dry eye, foreign-body sensation in the eye, punctate keratitis, and COVID-19. Seven participants had increased-IOP TEAEs. In 4, the event affected only the study eye and might have reflected waning implant efficacy. Two had increased IOP in both eyes at a sleep-lab visit, and 1 had increased IOP only in the fellow eye receiving standard care. Visual-field-defect TEAEs occurred in 3 participants: 1 had mild nasal-step visual progression in the study eye that the investigator judged unrelated to treatment, while the other 2 events affected standard-care fellow eyes. Most treatment-related TEAEs concerned the administration procedure; all TEAEs were mild or moderate. The sole serious TEAE was coronavirus disease 19 and was considered unrelated to treatment. No TEAE caused study discontinuation, and no implant required removal. Assessments identified no safety concerns involving best-corrected visual acuity, visual fields, lens opacity, cup/disc ratio, central corneal thickness, CECD, gonioscopy, or the implant. No clinically significant study-eye CECD change occurred. At month 12, mean (SD) change from baseline was -53.0 (95.74) cells/mm2, corresponding to a 2% mean CECD decline over 12 months; no eye lost 15% of baseline CECD. Gonioscopy indicated implant biodegradation. At week 16, 38.7% (12/31) of implants had swollen to an estimated 101% to 150% of initial size. By month 12, 67.7% (21/31) were no longer visible or were estimated at 25% of initial size; 29.0% (9/31) were estimated at 25% to 50%, and 3.2% (1/31) at 50% to 75%.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors interpreted their findings as showing that bimatoprost implant lowered IOP throughout 24 hours in OAG and OHT: habitual-position IOP fell consistently during daytime and nighttime at week 8, when 24-hour variation was also lower than at baseline. Earlier studies of once-daily topical bimatoprost 0.01% found daytime and nighttime IOP reductions, but their mean daytime reductions were approximately twice their nighttime reductions. In this study, mean habitual-position reductions were 2.6 mmHg by day and 2.1 mmHg by night. The authors interpreted this pattern as more sustained IOP lowering across 24 hours than with once-daily bimatoprost 0.01%, while acknowledging that their study did not support a direct comparison between groups. Prior evidence identifies long-term IOP variation as a risk factor for glaucomatous progression; an association between the size of short-term, 24-hour variation and progression risk is considered possible. Implant-treated study eyes had less 24-hour variation at week 8. Reference eyes did not show such a reduction, potentially because that cohort was small; previous studies had suggested that topical PGAs, including bimatoprost, reduce 24-hour IOP variation. Both sleep-lab pneumatonometry and office GAT detected lower 8 AM IOP at week 8, although their readings differed. The approximately 7 mmHg GAT reduction was consistent with the phase 3 ARTEMIS studies. The cause of the between-setting discrepancy was unknown. The authors noted different tonometry methods, prior reports that pneumatonometry overestimates IOP relative to GAT, and the effects of central corneal thickness on both methods and of IOP itself on pneumatonometry. Assessors and measurement days also differed. Follow-up after a single implant was longer than in ARTEMIS. Most participants maintained lower IOP for up to 1 year: 74% (23/31) had needed no further study-eye IOP-lowering treatment at 1 year. The authors compared this with a phase 1/2 implant study in which 28% (21/75) of recipients of 6-, 10-, 15-, or 20-mg implants completed 24 months without rescue topical medication or another study-eye implant. They proposed, rather than established, that persistently lower IOP after implant drug depletion could result from high target-tissue bimatoprost concentrations increasing matrix metalloproteinase activation and durably remodeling aqueous-outflow pathways. The implant was well tolerated in this study: no TEAE required removal or caused withdrawal, the most frequent events were ocular and mild or moderate, and no serious TEAE was treatment-related. At 1 year, no implant-treated eye had CECD loss of 15% or greater. The authors noted that CECD loss of 10% or less may be unreliable because of measurement error or may lack clinical importance, whereas greater losses can accompany reduced corneal transparency, edema, and poorer visual acuity. In the phase 3 ARTEMIS studies, approximately 5% of patients receiving the 10-mg implant had CECD loss of 20% or greater within 1 year after 3 administrations at fixed 16-week intervals; those studies reported no corneal endothelial-cell-loss TEAEs before the second 10-mg administration. Likewise, this single-administration study found no clinically significant CECD loss. A study strength was use of the same pneumatonometer and an assessor masked to study eye for each participant’s sleep-lab readings. This allowed habitual-position measurement without introducing daytime-versus-nighttime differences from switching tonometry methods within a participant. Limitations included the small sample and the absence of nighttime IOP measurements during undisturbed sleep. The reference cohort was intended to check whether measured topical-PGA IOP reductions aligned with earlier literature, not to support direct comparison: it was very small, came from one site, and assignment there was not randomized. Pneumatonometry and GAT hour-0 readings were taken on different days by different assessors and therefore could not be compared directly. Office IOP assessments were unmasked, although the 2-person reading method was intended to reduce bias. Reference-cohort efficacy and safety were not followed long term because that cohort exited at 8 weeks. In summary, the authors concluded that one implant lowered IOP throughout day and night, reduced 24-hour IOP variation, and had a favorable safety profile through 1 year. Most patients maintained lower study-eye IOP without further treatment across the 12-month study; the authors judged the probability of needing no other IOP-lowering treatment for at least 1 year to be high.
